defEn: A countermeasure that monitors endpoints such as PCs, servers and smart devices and prevents the intrusion of malware and ransomware. Japan's Digital Agency positions it as one of the Zero Trust functions of “checking the state of resources”.
howEn: It continuously monitors the behavior of files and processes on the endpoint, and also uses machine learning on the cloud side to detect and block threats. For example, Microsoft Defender Antivirus stops malicious code using local and cloud machine learning, behavioral analysis and heuristics, and blocks new threats almost immediately.
diffEn: Whereas EDR handles detection and response after an intrusion, EPP is on the side that prevents the intrusion itself. For example, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint provides preventive defense and post-intrusion detection and response in a single endpoint platform.
aiEn: Microsoft's next-generation protection includes a capability that blocks attacks on local AI agents running on the endpoint by monitoring the agent's operating loop. Defending the endpoints that run AI is also within the scope of EPP.

defEn: A mechanism that monitors the operations and behavior of endpoints (PCs, servers, smart devices, etc.), discovers that a cyberattack has occurred and responds as soon as it is found. Assuming that intrusion will happen, it is responsible for post-intrusion detection and containment.
howEn: It continuously collects behavioral data such as processes, network communications, logins, and changes to the registry and files. For example, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint groups alerts for the same attack technique or the same attacker into a single incident, investigates by looking back through 6 months of data, and responds by means such as isolating the endpoint.
diffEn: The main role of EPP is preventing intrusion, and that of EDR is post-intrusion detection and response. Whereas EDR looks at endpoint behavior, XDR correlates signals from multiple domains such as identity, email and apps, in addition to endpoints.
aiEn: Because the behavior of endpoints that use generative AI can also be traced after the fact, it serves as investigative material for suspicious operations that went through AI tools. When introducing AI, include the status of EDR deployment on the target endpoints among the items to check.

defEn: Integrated defense that coordinates detection, prevention, investigation and response across multiple domains such as endpoints, identity, email and applications. For example, Microsoft Defender XDR is an integrated defense suite that covers both pre-intrusion and post-intrusion.
howEn: It links the alerts and suspicious events from each product into a single incident, so that the intrusion path and the affected assets can be followed on one screen. Microsoft Defender XDR correlates high-confidence signals from multiple products to contain attacks automatically, and lets you search the past 30 days of raw data across products.
diffEn: EDR specializes in endpoint behavior. XDR adds signals from identity, email and cloud apps to that and correlates them. Whereas SIEM collects and analyzes logs from across the whole organization and raises alerts, XDR goes as far as the detection and response of each product, as one integrated whole.
aiEn: Because signals from endpoints, identity and cloud apps can be followed together, it is a foundation for investigating, across domains, suspicious sign-ins and endpoint behavior linked to the use of generative AI services.

fullEn: Managed Detection and Response (outsourced monitoring and response operations service)
defEn: A service in which specialist analysts take over the operation of detection and response. For example, in Microsoft Defender Experts MDR, analysts manage the incident queue on a 24-hour basis, carry out investigations on the customer's behalf, and either respond themselves or guide the customer's response.
howEn: It is positioned to supplement, not replace, the customer's security operations center (SOC), reducing the volume of alerts to be handled so that people can be devoted to the threats that affect the organization. Plan 2 of the service extends its scope to the logs of some third-party products collected in Microsoft Sentinel.
diffEn: EDR and XDR are tools for detection and response, while MDR is a service in which people operate using them. The service does not include the incident response work itself after a breach has occurred; a separate service is provided for that.
aiEn: It is an option when the number of monitored targets grows with the introduction of generative AI but your own SOC lacks staff. Before contracting, confirm the scope of covered products and logs, and the division of roles with your own company.

fullEn: Mobile Device Management / Unified Endpoint Management
defEn: Tools for comprehensively managing mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets. In the Digital Agency's materials it is written as EMM (MDM), and it is positioned as the function that makes endpoints identifiable under Zero Trust.
howEn: For example, Microsoft Intune enrolls, configures and updates Android, iOS/iPadOS, Linux, macOS and Windows devices in the same cloud service, and can wipe a device if it is lost. It passes the device's compliance state to conditional access, so access from non-compliant devices can be stopped.
diffEn: MDM manages the whole device, while MAM manages only business apps and the data within them. MAM is for personally owned devices (BYOD), and can selectively wipe only the organization's data when someone leaves the company.
aiEn: If device compliance state is linked to conditional access, you can operate so that only managed devices are allowed to use business data and generative AI services. Personally owned devices are protected with MAM, limited to the data inside apps.

defEn: Vulnerability management is the activity of identifying and assessing vulnerabilities and misconfigurations, fixing them, and tracking them. Patch management refers to the operation of distributing and applying, in a planned manner, updates, which are the main means of that remediation, to endpoints and servers.
howEn: For example, Microsoft Defender Vulnerability Management continuously inventories software, certificates, browser extensions and so on, and prompts remediation by prioritizing vulnerabilities that are actually being exploited and important assets. Deployment is rolled out in stages with Intune update rings, and urgent updates can override deferral settings and be distributed immediately.
diffEn: Patch management is the work of applying updates, while vulnerability management includes finding which ones should be fixed and prioritizing them. When an update cannot be applied, other mitigations are taken, such as configuration changes or blocking vulnerable apps.
aiEn: Include client software and browser extensions related to generative AI in the inventory as well. Not leaving out of the register the software on endpoints that grows with AI adoption is the premise for preventing missed updates.

defEn: A countermeasure that defines by policy the code allowed to run on an endpoint and does not run anything that is not permitted. Instead of stopping what antivirus judges to be malicious, it takes the approach of running only what has been allowed.
howEn: Windows has App Control for Business and AppLocker. The scope covers not only apps but also scripts, MSI, batch files and interactive PowerShell sessions, and code running in the kernel can also be restricted. There are also methods that let through only signed code or code that a cloud reputation service predicts to be safe.
diffEn: Whereas EPP and antivirus judge whether something is malicious and stop it, application control runs only the code that has been allowed. The source states that it is not a substitute for antivirus and should be used together with it.
aiEn: As a deployment policy, you can decide whether to include AI clients and development tools that run on endpoints in the allow list. A state in which only permitted executables run is a means of curbing the introduction of unapproved tools.

fullEn: Device Control (control of peripheral device use)
defEn: A countermeasure that controls by policy whether peripherals such as USB drives, printers and Bluetooth devices can be installed and used on an endpoint. It narrows the channels for data exfiltration and malware intrusion.
howEn: Windows' standard device installation restrictions decide allow and deny by device ID or setup class. In the Defender for Endpoint example, you can specify in fine detail the device type, read/write/execute, user group, network location and file type, and there is also a setting that allows only media encrypted with BitLocker.
diffEn: Whereas DLP stops exfiltration based on content such as the sensitivity of documents, device control stops it by device type and attributes. The source also says that Endpoint DLP is used to prevent copying to USB based on sensitivity.
aiEn: It is a means of closing the route by which source data, before it is handed to AI, is taken out via USB or printing. It is positioned as a layer that manages the physical exits of the endpoint, separate from input controls for generative AI.

fullEn: Full Disk Encryption (encryption of an endpoint's entire disk; e.g. BitLocker)
defEn: A countermeasure that encrypts an endpoint's entire volume to prevent data from being read through loss, theft or improper disposal. Windows' standard feature is BitLocker, and it is basically used in combination with a TPM.
howEn: In combination with a TPM, it can also verify that the endpoint was not tampered with while it was shut down. A PIN or startup key can be required at boot to make it multi-factor. With device encryption, BitLocker is enabled automatically and the recovery key is stored in places such as Microsoft Entra ID or AD DS.
diffEn: Whereas encryption and key management (KMS, HSM) is a framework that deals with generating and storing keys, disk encryption is an individual countermeasure that protects an endpoint's volume. It is not something that judges exfiltration by content, as DLP does.
aiEn: In operations where AI validation data or internal documents are brought onto endpoints, assume as a premise that they cannot be read if the endpoint is lost. The storage location of recovery keys also becomes something to manage.

fullEn: Secure Boot / Trusted Boot / Measured Boot (integrity verification at startup)
defEn: A mechanism that verifies that each component of the boot process has not been tampered with, in order to prevent bootkits and rootkits that run before the OS starts. It protects the stage before the security features on the OS start working.
howEn: In Windows, Secure Boot loads only trusted boot loaders, and Trusted Boot verifies the signatures of boot components such as the kernel. ELAM inspects drivers, and Measured Boot saves a record of the boot in the TPM and, by sending it to a trusted server, allows the endpoint's health to be assessed.
diffEn: Whereas device compliance evaluates rules about settings and state, Measured Boot is a record of the boot, which makes it possible to see through an infected endpoint even if it declares itself normal.
aiEn: Use it as the premise that endpoints handling AI or confidential data have not been tampered with. It can be tied to a design that admits to the internal network only endpoints whose trusted boot has been verified.

fullEn: Device Compliance (evaluation of endpoint compliance status)
defEn: A mechanism that evaluates whether managed devices meet the configuration requirements set by the organization and determines whether they are compliant or non-compliant. If the result is used for access control, only devices that meet the requirements can be allowed to use business resources.
howEn: In the Intune example, rules such as the minimum OS version, the absence of jailbreaking or rooting, and the threat level are distributed to devices. For non-compliant devices, actions such as notification, remote lock and retire are taken. The result is reported to Entra ID, and conditional access allows only compliant devices.
diffEn: Conditional access is the control that decides whether to allow access, and device compliance is the evaluation of device state used in that decision. MDM / UEM is the platform that manages devices, and the evaluation is one of its functions.
aiEn: It can be used to design the devices permitted to use generative AI for work so that they are limited to compliant devices. It serves as input for the decision when you want to stop the use of AI services from personal devices.

defEn: A method in which desktops and apps are run on servers in a data center or the cloud and only the screen is delivered to the user's endpoint. By keeping the actual processing and data outside the endpoint, it lets users use the same environment regardless of the device they have at hand.
howEn: In the Azure Virtual Desktop example, either a full Windows desktop or individual apps (RemoteApp) are delivered, and users connect with a dedicated client or the HTML5 Web client. Because connections are established to the service as reverse connections, there is no need to open inbound ports. Administrators manage the images and virtual machines.
diffEn: Whereas MDM manages settings on the endpoint side, VDI manages the OS and apps on the delivery side. It makes it easy to let people use the same environment regardless of endpoint type, but operating the infrastructure for screen delivery is required.
aiEn: It is an option for distributing, in an isolated form, the working environment in which AI tools are used. However, introducing VDI does not in itself constitute a countermeasure against exfiltration; control of copying and printing must be designed separately.

fullEn: IT Asset Inventory / Discovery (inventory and visualization of IT assets)
defEn: An activity of identifying, without omission, the endpoints, network devices and IoT on the organization's network and compiling them in a register. Unmanaged devices become vulnerability loopholes without ever being included among what is protected.
howEn: In the Defender for Endpoint device discovery example, onboarded endpoints passively observe network communications and, as needed, actively probe, then find unmanaged endpoints, devices such as routers, and IoT such as printers, and add them to the list. Authenticated scans via SNMP can also assess vulnerabilities in network devices.
diffEn: Whereas MDM / UEM manages registered endpoints, asset inventory includes discovering unregistered devices. Whereas shadow IT mainly refers to the unauthorized use of cloud services, this centers on devices.
aiEn: It is a foundation for identifying the endpoints, servers and devices where AI is being used or developed. Assets that cannot be identified are also left out of the scope of AI adoption risk assessment.

fullEn: Security Baseline / Configuration Hardening (applying recommended settings and configuration management)
defEn: An initiative to decide in advance a set of security-recommended settings for the OS and apps, and to apply and maintain them in the same state on all endpoints. It reduces configuration weaknesses and variation between endpoints, and brings them into a uniform hardened state.
howEn: Intune security baselines distribute templates preconfigured with recommended values to groups, and they can be adjusted to the organization's circumstances. By default, they enable, for example, BitLocker for removable drives and a password on device unlock. Version updates and checking for conflicts with other policies are the key operational points.
diffEn: Patch management is the work of applying updates, while a baseline is the work of aligning settings. The source says that Intune baselines do not strictly conform to CIS or NIST and are used as a starting point after adjustment.
aiEn: The source's list of baselines also includes one for AI agents running on endpoints (preview). Set standards for the settings of the AI execution environment and manage it in the same way as other endpoints.

defEn: A mechanism that enables the right people, machines and software to access the right resources at the right time. It first has the user prove who they are, and then allows or denies access to resources.
howEn: It consists of identity creation and management, federation, granting and revoking user access (provisioning), authentication, authorization, access control, and reporting and monitoring. Identities are issued not only to people but also to workloads, devices and AI agents.
diffEn: Authentication is verifying identity and authorization is deciding what someone may do; they are separate processes. IAM is the framework that includes both; IdP, SSO and MFA are its components, and PAM is the area specialized for privileges.
aiEn: Mechanisms such as Microsoft Entra Agent ID, which give AI agents independent identities and authenticate, authorize and govern them, are emerging. When introducing generative AI, include in the IAM design which identity the AI uses and what it is made to do.

fullEn: Identity Provider / Identity as a Service (cloud-based identity management)
defEn: An IdP is a mechanism that creates, maintains and manages identity information and provides authentication, authorization and audit services. IDaaS refers to a cloud-based form that centrally manages identities configured separately for multiple systems and also manages access rights appropriately.
howEn: Apps delegate user authentication to the IdP, and users sign in to each app with a common identity. The IdP centrally handles setting policies, monitoring user behavior and detecting suspicious activity, which reduces the need for each app to hold its own IDs and passwords.
diffEn: IdP refers to the role that handles authentication, and IDaaS to the form of provision in which it is used as a cloud service. IAM is a higher-level framework that includes the IdP, and the app is on the side that receives and uses the IdP's authentication result.
aiEn: Azure's design guidance recommends using a trusted IdP rather than building your own identity platform. Consolidate authentication for generative AI services in the IdP as well, and do not increase individual per-service accounts.

defEn: A mechanism in which, once a user has signed in, they can access multiple assigned applications without signing in again. Authentication is performed by the IdP, and the apps receive the authentication result and allow use.
howEn: The app sends the user to the IdP, and the IdP verifies the credentials and tells the app that the user is who they claim to be. The representative integration methods are SAML 2.0, which is XML-based, and OIDC, which uses JSON tokens on OAuth 2.0; for apps that do not support them, there is also a method in which the IdP stores the credentials and enters them on the user's behalf.
diffEn: SSO is a mechanism that reduces re-authentication and centralizes management, while MFA is a mechanism that raises authentication strength; their purposes differ and they are used together. SAML suits traditional Web apps, and OIDC suits new Web apps, mobile and APIs.
aiEn: If generative AI services are placed under SSO, applying usage policies and cutting off access can be done in one place on the IdP side. When choosing an enterprise generative AI service, include SSO support among the requirements.

defEn: An authentication method that requires another type of identity verification in addition to the password at sign-in. The factors are divided into “something you know”, “something you have” and “something you are (biometrics)”, and 2 or more types are combined.
howEn: With a password alone, an attacker can use it if it is weak or has been leaked elsewhere. The second factor is difficult for an attacker to obtain or duplicate, so security improves. Examples of methods are authenticator apps, FIDO2 passkeys, hardware keys, and SMS or voice calls.
diffEn: MFA is about the strength of authentication, while SSO is a mechanism that reduces the number of authentications; their purposes differ. Conditional access is on the side that decides in which situations MFA is required: on the internal network a normal sign-in is used, while from outside or on personal devices an additional factor is required.
aiEn: The Digital Agency lists making MFA mandatory for all users as a measure when the risk of identity verification is high. For administrators of generative AI services, and for users who connect with internal data, make MFA mandatory first.

defEn: A mechanism that, when a user accesses a resource, gathers signals such as the user, location, device, app and risk, and decides whether to allow, to require additional requirements, or to deny. Policies are written in the form “if ..., then ...”.
howEn: For example, Microsoft Entra Conditional Access evaluates policies after first-factor authentication. The decision is either to block, or to grant access while requiring MFA, a compliant device, a password change or the like; typical examples are requiring MFA for administrator roles and blocking legacy authentication.
diffEn: MFA is a means of additional identity verification, while conditional access is the control that decides, according to the situation, whether to require it. Whereas authorization by role decides “who can do what”, conditional access narrows the entrance by circumstances such as device and location.
aiEn: Microsoft Entra Conditional Access can also target the identities of AI agents (as of November 2026, Entra Agent ID is generally available, while targeting agent user accounts is still in preview), extending Zero Trust principles to AI workloads. On the user side as well, conditions such as “allow only compliant devices” can be set.

defEn: A mechanism that manages and governs privileged accounts such as administrators and privileged access to critical systems. In addition to human privileged accounts, application and service accounts are also covered.
howEn: It is governed through just-in-time (JIT) access, which grants privileges only while needed, time-bound assignments with start and end dates, approval, MFA at activation, entering a reason, access reviews, and audit history. For example, Microsoft Entra Privileged Identity Management provides these.
diffEn: Whereas ordinary IAM handles the access of all users, PAM narrows to high-impact administrator privileges, avoiding standing assignment and restricting by time and approval. It is also positioned as an operational means of applying the principle of least privilege to privileges.
aiEn: Administrator privileges on AI platforms and service accounts called by AI can also become privileges. Include in the design an operation in which these are not assigned permanently and are activated only when needed.

defEn: An activity of consistently managing the creation, change, and disabling or deletion of accounts and access rights in step with joining, transfer and leaving the company. It includes both granting (provisioning) and revoking (deprovisioning).
howEn: For example, the Microsoft Entra provisioning service creates, updates and deletes users and groups through the app's SCIM 2.0 API. The targets are determined by assignment and group membership; users who fall out of scope are disabled by default, and deleted identities are also deleted on the app side.
diffEn: SSO deals with “which identity to sign in with”, while provisioning via SCIM deals with “the creation and disabling of the account itself”. SCIM is the standard protocol used for that integration.
aiEn: Azure's design guidance calls for not leaving identity access in place longer than the lifetime of the resource, and for removing the permissions of departed employees through access reviews. Make generative AI service accounts subject to the same inventory.

defEn: An operating principle of giving each user only the minimum privileges required for the work they are responsible for. The Digital Agency presents as Zero Trust the idea of evaluating and enforcing, through access control rules, that access between resources satisfies this principle.
howEn: Assign to a role only the privileges needed to complete the work, and narrow the scope to the extent of the job duties. Ask whether read-only is enough, start from the minimum privileges and add as needed. Avoid permissions tied to individual resources or individuals, and manage with built-in roles and groups.
diffEn: JIT narrows the time during which privileges are held, and least privilege narrows the size of the privileges. Combining the two can reduce the scope of impact when an identity is compromised.
aiEn: In the Microsoft Entra Agent ID example, each AI agent is given a governed identity, made to access with least privilege, and its actions leave an audit trail. When connecting data to generative AI, also start from read-only.

defEn: A method of verifying identity not with a password but with credentials that use public-key cryptography. Based on FIDO standards, the private key stays on the device and can be used only on the site or app where it was registered, so it is hard to steal through phishing.
howEn: At sign-in, the server sends a random number (challenge); when the user unlocks the device's private key with biometrics or a PIN, a signature is returned. The server verifies the signature with the public key and issues a token. There are types that are bound to the device and types that are synchronized in the cloud, and the synchronized type does not support attestation.
diffEn: Ordinary MFA is a method that adds something like an SMS code to the password, and it can be stolen through phishing. With passkeys, the credential is bound to the destination, so it cannot be handed over to a fake site. It is also one means of realizing MFA.
aiEn: The source states that phishing has become more sophisticated and larger in scale with attack tools that use AI. It is a basis for moving to phishing-resistant authentication, starting with administrators of AI services and users who handle confidential data.

defEn: An initiative that detects attacks targeting identities through analysis of behavior such as sign-ins and privilege changes, and goes as far as investigation and response. In addition to human identities, it also covers non-human identities such as service accounts and apps for protection.
howEn: In the Defender for Identity example, signals are collected from on-premises AD, Entra ID and other IAM, and behavioral analysis and known attack patterns are used to detect reconnaissance, credential compromise, lateral movement, domain dominance and so on. Responses include disabling a compromised account, revoking sessions, and resetting credentials.
diffEn: Whereas IAM and PAM are on the side that grants and restricts privileges, ITDR is on the side that detects suspicious behavior and responds. It handles containment per identity, such as disabling a compromised account.
aiEn: The source treats service accounts, service principals and AI agent identities, in addition to human identities, as protection targets. It can also be used to detect abnormal behavior of the non-human identities that AI uses.

fullEn: Identity Federation (identity linking and trust relationships)
defEn: A mechanism that establishes an authentication trust relationship between organizations or systems, so that users can sign in to and use another organization's apps or other systems with the account they hold in their own organization or at an external identity provider.
howEn: Trust is set up with the other party's IdP using SAML, WS-Fed or the like; the user is redirected from the app to their own IdP, authenticates, and returns with the result. Configuration is required on both sides, registering the issuer URI, the authentication endpoint and the signing certificate. If there is a metadata URL, certificates can be renewed automatically; if not, they are renewed manually.
diffEn: SSO refers to the experience of a user using multiple apps with a single authentication, and federation is the trust relationship that makes that work across organizations. The source says that B2B accounts for guests do not become unnecessary even with federation.
aiEn: When business partners or contractors enter an AI-related environment, it can be chosen as a way to let them use their own identities. Even in this case, your own side needs to manage the guest's privileges and validity period.

defEn: RBAC is a method of granting privileges together to roles. ABAC is a method of deciding whether to allow access based on the attributes of the user, the resource and the environment. Both are design models for access control (authorization).
howEn: In Azure RBAC, privileges are granted by role assignments consisting of 3 elements, a principal, a role definition and a scope, and the effect is the sum of the assignments. Azure ABAC adds conditions to this, for example allowing reads only of Blobs that carry a specific tag. It can also reduce the number of assignments.
diffEn: RBAC can be implemented simply in line with business operations, and ABAC can narrow things down finely by attributes. The source says that using both together gives advanced authorization. Least privilege is a principle, and RBAC and ABAC are methods for realizing it.
aiEn: It can be used to design the internal data that AI references so that it is narrowed not only by role but also by attributes such as confidentiality classification and project. It becomes the premise that AI does not pull documents beyond a person's privileges.

fullEn: Non-Human Identity / Workload Identity (identities assigned to apps, services, etc.)
defEn: An identity assigned to software such as apps, services, scripts and containers so that it can authenticate to and access other services and resources. It is the identity of a machine rather than a person, and is a kind of non-human identity alongside device identities.
howEn: In Entra, applications, service principals and managed identities correspond to this. Managed identities eliminate the need to manage credentials, and workload identity federation enables authentication without secrets in places such as GitHub Actions. Conditional access, ID Protection and access reviews can also be applied.
diffEn: Whereas a person uses 1 identity to get into multiple resources, a workload holds multiple credentials per resource, and it is hard to keep track of their creation and revocation. The source points out that attackers tend to target non-human identities.
aiEn: The source treats AI agents as a separate kind of machine identity and provides a dedicated identity with a human sponsor, lifecycle management and bulk policy application. It becomes the center of inventory and privilege design for identities when AI calls APIs.

fullEn: Secrets Management (secure storage and distribution of passwords, API keys and certificates)
defEn: An initiative to store confidential information such as tokens, passwords, certificates and API keys centrally in a dedicated vault, instead of writing it in the app's code or configuration files, and to control access to it. It reduces opportunities for leakage.
howEn: In the Azure Key Vault example, the app accesses the vault by URI and retrieves the secret it needs. Access is authenticated with Entra ID and authorized with Azure RBAC and the like. The vault is encrypted at rest with HSM keys, and usage records are kept in logs and can be monitored. Vaults can be separated per app to narrow access.
diffEn: Whereas encryption and key management (KMS, HSM) protect the keys for data encryption, secrets management holds credentials used by apps in general. Key Vault can be used for both, but the purposes differ.
aiEn: Design AI apps so that they retrieve external API keys and model connection information from a vault instead of embedding them in code. Tie the keys to non-human identities and limit them to minimum privileges.

fullEn: Access Review / Access Recertification (periodic review of access rights)
defEn: An activity in which the responsible person or the user themselves periodically confirms whether the access rights given to users are still needed, and removes the unneeded ones. It prevents excessive privileges from remaining, and prevents being cited in an audit as a control deficiency.
howEn: In the Entra example, reviews are created for group members, app assignments, roles and access packages. They can recur from weekly to yearly, and reviewers choose to approve or deny. It suits situations such as checking the number of people in privileged roles and the remaining external guests.
diffEn: Whereas identity lifecycle management automatically grants and revokes in line with changes of joining, transfer and leaving, access review is where people reconfirm privileges that automation cannot catch. It also complements the time limits of PAM.
aiEn: Include administrator roles on AI platforms, and service principals given privileges for AI, among the review targets as well. The source states that reviewing service principals assigned to privileged roles is also possible.

defEn: A system, or a device on which it is implemented, installed at the point connecting the external network and the internal network to prevent unauthorized intrusion from outside. It is the basic defense at the network perimeter.
howEn: It decides according to rules whether to pass or block communications. Azure Firewall, an example of the cloud type, inspects from L3 to L7 and can restrict destinations in units of FQDN or URL. Premium also provides intrusion detection and prevention (IDPS) and TLS inspection, and Microsoft positions it as an NGFW.
diffEn: Whereas a general firewall monitors at the network level, a WAF monitors Web application communications at the application level. DDoS protection mitigates overload attacks, separately from decisions on whether to allow communications.
aiEn: It is a foundation for allowing or denying, in units of destination FQDN or URL, communications going from inside the company out to external generative AI services. Per-user control and data exfiltration countermeasures are handled by SWG and CASB.

fullEn: Intrusion Detection System / Intrusion Prevention System
defEn: An IDS is a system that identifies packets arriving from the network, detects unauthorized intrusions and attacks, and notifies the administrator. An IPS, in addition to detection, has a function of automatically blocking unauthorized packets.
howEn: They identify packets to find unauthorized access, and the IDS contacts the administrator by a predetermined method such as email or an alarm. The IPS blocks automatically. The IDPS of Azure Firewall Premium, a product example, detects attacks by patterns such as byte sequences and known malicious instruction sequences, records and reports them, and also blocks depending on settings.
diffEn: The difference is that an IDS goes as far as detecting and notifying, while an IPS goes as far as blocking. Separately from a firewall's allow/deny rules, they have the role of distinguishing attacks from communication patterns.
aiEn: If you place a generative AI or RAG platform in the cloud, they can be used as a layer that watches for suspicious behavior at the platform's entrance and in internal traffic. At the time of introduction, also decide on an operation that does not stop legitimate communications through false positives.

defEn: A firewall that monitors communications with the outside for Web applications and defends against attacks on vulnerabilities and theft of information. Unlike a general firewall, it monitors at the application level.
howEn: It checks the contents of requests against rules, allowing or blocking them, and prevents things such as SQL injection. Azure WAF, a product example, is built into Application Gateway and Front Door. The advantage is said to be that known vulnerabilities can be handled in one place with the WAF instead of being fixed in each app.
diffEn: A firewall monitors at the network level and a WAF at the application level. Because Azure DDoS Protection protects L3/L4, a WAF needs to be added for Web app defense (L7).
aiEn: If you have a generative AI chat UI or API exposed inside or outside the company, it serves as a layer that prevents typical Web attacks at the entrance. Countermeasures for AI-specific input such as prompts should be considered separately.

defEn: A technology, or the equipment for it, that achieves a situation like a dedicated-line connection over a shared network such as the Internet by means of encryption and traffic control. Remote access VPN refers to the use of connecting from endpoints such as those at home to the organization's network.
howEn: A teleworking endpoint makes a VPN connection to the office network, and connects to internal file servers and cloud services to do work. Because cloud use also passes through the office's security devices, a level equivalent to that inside the office can be maintained. Because data can be stored on the endpoint, countermeasures against loss and removal are required.
diffEn: Microsoft positions conventional VPN as something that grants broad network access with certificates alone. It presents an approach of gradually replacing it with ZTNA, which allows access per app by looking at identity and context.
aiEn: It serves as the route for reaching, remotely, generative AI placed inside the company and internal data integration platforms. Because VPN tends to reach a wide range, also consider separating the AI platform into its own zone and narrowing access down with ZTNA.

defEn: A computer or software placed between a company's or organization's internal network and the Internet, which connects to the Internet as a proxy on behalf of internal computers that cannot connect to the Internet directly.
howEn: Users' browsers and the like are configured to send communications through the proxy, and communication to external sites is carried out by the proxy on their behalf. Azure Firewall explicit proxy, a product example, distributes settings manually or by PAC file, and handles HTTP and HTTPS. For teleworking, a configuration in which authentication and access control are performed by a proxy on the cloud is presented.
diffEn: Whereas a proxy is a mechanism that acts on behalf of internal-to-external communications, SWG refers to a cloud-based form of it that evaluates the safety of the destination URL or IP address and blocks if it is not safe.
aiEn: If communications to generative AI services are gathered at the proxy, you can create an egress that passes only permitted services and keeps a record of use. In the case of local breakout, apply equivalent control with a cloud proxy.

defEn: A mechanism that blocks malicious domains at the stage of DNS name resolution. DNS is the mechanism that converts domain names into IP addresses; by stopping name resolution, which is the entrance of communication, it prevents damage.
howEn: Allow, block and alert rules are set against lists of domains. Azure DNS resolver policy, a product example, can filter and log DNS queries per virtual network, and block known malicious domains derived from MSRC at name resolution. Microsoft explains that almost all attacks start from a DNS query.
diffEn: Among the components of SWG, Web filtering (blocking malicious Web pages) and DNS filtering (blocking malicious domains) line up as separate items. With DNS, the unit of judgment is the domain.
aiEn: It can be used as a means to stop the domains of unapproved generative AI services at the name resolution stage. Blocking per service is the main use, and the content of use within permitted services is viewed by other mechanisms such as CASB.

fullEn: Static IP address / IP address allow list
defEn: Fixing the IP address used as the connection source to an unchanging value. The receiving side can narrow the access source by “IP address restriction (allow list)”, which allows only that IP address. A dynamic IP can change on stop or reassignment.
howEn: For cloud services and administrator privileges where it can be configured, narrowing the access source by IP address restriction is recommended (Japan's Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications). Azure static IPs are used to update the other party's firewall rules and to communicate with other services that use IP-address-based security.
diffEn: Microsoft states that via a cloud proxy or VPN, the IP seen by the destination becomes the egress of each service, and keeping an up-to-date list is difficult. This is supplemented with device compliance conditions and with source IP restoration, which conveys the original IP. In Conditional Access, network location is one decision input alongside other conditions.
aiEn: When an internal system calls an external generative AI API, if the other party requires an allow list of source IPs, fixing the egress IP is a prerequisite. Do not rely on IP alone; combine it with authentication and device state.

defEn: A mechanism that translates between internal private IP addresses and the global IP addresses used on the Internet. With SNAT, which rewrites the source, multiple internal devices can connect externally with the same public IP address.
howEn: SNAT rewrites the source IP and port into a public IP and port pair, and distinguishes connections by port number. Azure NAT Gateway is for outbound communication only; it does not accept connections initiated from outside and passes only response packets. When ports run out, new connections fail.
diffEn: NAT is a mechanism that rewrites addresses, and its role differs from a firewall that judges whether communication is permitted. With SNAT, multiple devices share the public IP, so the destination sees only the egress IP address, not the individual devices.
aiEn: When an internal system calls an external generative AI API, the source seen by the destination is the NAT's egress IP. If the other party requires an allow list of source IPs, fix this egress IP.

defEn: A design that divides a network into segments (zones) and controls communications per zone to limit the spread of damage. Micro-segmentation is the finer division down to the unit of workload or app, and restricts the lateral movement of attackers.
howEn: In the Azure example, subnets and virtual networks are separated per app or component, only communications from the necessary parties are allowed by NSG rules, and inspection is performed by Azure Firewall placed in the hub. Whether the division is as intended is verified with Traffic Analytics, which analyzes flow logs.
diffEn: Macro-segmentation is large zones by function or security requirements, and micro-segmentation divides finely inside them. Microsoft lists as a principle adopting identity-based segmentation rather than the conventional IP-based one.
aiEn: If you place the generative AI platform, reference data and business systems in separate zones and allow only the necessary communications, you can curb the spread from the AI platform to business data in the event of a compromise.

fullEn: DDoS Protection (countermeasures against distributed denial-of-service attacks)
defEn: A DDoS attack sends a large volume of service requests from multiple computers, placing excessive load on a server or network and making it unusable. DDoS protection refers to mechanisms that detect and mitigate this attack.
howEn: Azure DDoS Protection, a product example, monitors traffic patterns 24 hours a day and mitigates automatically when it detects signs of an attack. It automatically adjusts thresholds by learning traffic volume, and the protected targets are resources that have public IP addresses. A redundant design and a response plan are used together.
diffEn: A DoS attack is carried out from 1 computer, whereas a DDoS attack is carried out simultaneously from multiple machines such as third-party computers infected with bots. In terms of products, DDoS Protection protects L3/L4, and the Web application layer (L7) is complemented by a WAF.
aiEn: A published generative AI chat UI or API can be a target of attacks aimed at availability. If you have a public endpoint, include both L3/L4 mitigation and an L7 WAF in the design.

fullEn: Email authentication (verifying the email sender with SPF, DKIM and DMARC)
defEn: A general term for technologies by which the receiving side verifies whether the sender domain of an email has been spoofed. SPF, DKIM and DMARC are combined to distinguish spoofed emails and phishing.
howEn: SPF indicates, in a DNS TXT record, the senders permitted to send email for that domain. DKIM attaches a digital signature to the email header, and the receiving side checks for tampering. DMARC checks alignment with the domain of the From address, and specifies the handling on failure and the reporting destination.
diffEn: SPF looks only at the MAIL FROM domain, and DKIM allows the signing domain to differ from From. DMARC's alignment check fills this gap, so the three are used in combination rather than alone.
aiEn: When AI agents or SaaS integrations send email automatically, authentication may fail unless that sending service is added to SPF or made to sign with DKIM using your own domain.

fullEn: Transport Layer Security / Public Key Infrastructure (communication encryption and public key infrastructure)
defEn: TLS is a protocol that encrypts communications and prevents spoofing. PKI is a mechanism in which a third-party certificate authority registers, issues and revokes digital certificates, and guarantees the binding between a public key and its owner. It is the successor to SSL.
howEn: The server presents a server certificate bearing the CA's signature, and the client confirms the authenticity of the destination by whether it can trace back to a root certificate it trusts. After confirmation, communication is encrypted. The certificate authority handles registering, issuing and revoking certificates, and there is also a method of operating your own internal certificate authority such as AD CS.
diffEn: Whereas encryption and key management (KMS) mainly deals with the operation of keys for stored data, TLS / PKI confirms with certificates that the communication partner is genuine and then encrypts the communication.
aiEn: Communications of generative AI APIs and between agents are also protected by TLS. Because the authenticity of the destination depends on certificate verification, management of issuance, renewal and revocation is an operational requirement.

fullEn: TLS inspection (decrypting and inspecting encrypted communications)
defEn: A mechanism in which a firewall or proxy temporarily terminates and decrypts encrypted HTTPS communications, inspects the contents, then re-encrypts and sends them on. It is used to find unauthorized communications hidden by encryption.
howEn: In the Azure Firewall Premium example, 2 TLS connections are established, one with the Web server and one with the client, and a temporary server certificate is created with a CA certificate provided by the customer. After decryption, IDPS and URL filtering work. Categories such as finance and healthcare can be excluded from decryption.
diffEn: IDS / IPS and WAF are functions that look at the contents of communications, and TLS inspection is the pre-processing that enables them to see the contents of encrypted communications. Without decryption, the inside of an encrypted tunnel cannot be seen.
aiEn: Communications to generative AI services are also HTTPS, so the content sent cannot be inspected unless decrypted. On the other hand, there is also a recommendation to exclude trusted destinations such as Microsoft 365 from decryption, so the scope needs to be designed.

fullEn: Private connectivity (non-public connection via closed networks, dedicated lines and Private Link)
defEn: A general term for connection methods that link to the cloud or to sites without passing communications through the public Internet, using a carrier's closed network or dedicated line, or private IP addresses within a virtual network. IP-VPN is also one of these.
howEn: ExpressRoute connects on-premises and the cloud through a private connection via a connectivity provider, and you can choose any-to-any (IP-VPN) or dedicated Ethernet. A private endpoint brings a service such as PaaS into your own network as a NIC with a private IP of the virtual network.
diffEn: Whereas VPN sets up an encrypted tunnel over a public network, with private connectivity the route itself does not go out to the public network. A private endpoint does not automatically stop access from the public side, so a separate control is required.
aiEn: AI search and machine learning services are listed among the target resources of private endpoints, and it can be used to design AI platforms that handle internal data so that they are not exposed to the Internet.

defEn: A mechanism that authenticates endpoints trying to connect to the network, checks whether they are registered and whether they conform to policy, and then controls whether to permit the connection. It is used at the entrance of wired LAN, Wi-Fi and VPN.
howEn: IEEE 802.1X requires authentication when connecting to a LAN port or Wi-Fi, and refuses the connection if it fails. NAC products query Intune and the like about the endpoint's enrollment and compliance state, guide non-conforming endpoints to enrollment or remediation, and permit the connection once they conform.
diffEn: Whereas conditional access decides on access to cloud apps, NAC decides at the point of connecting to a network such as the internal Wi-Fi or VPN. The two are used in coordination.
aiEn: It is a foundation for limiting the endpoints that can enter the internal network or VPN to managed ones, and can narrow the route by which AI is reached via internal data from unmanaged endpoints.

fullEn: Wireless LAN security (authentication and encryption for wireless LAN)
defEn: A mechanism that combines authentication at connection time and encryption of communications to prevent unauthorized connection to a wireless LAN (Wi-Fi) and eavesdropping on communications. WPA-family methods and IEEE 802.1X are central.
howEn: WPA is an encryption method that compensates for the weaknesses of WEP, and has WPA-PSK for home use and WPA-EAP for enterprise. The enterprise type queries an authentication server about the user with 802.1X and EAP, and manages keys dynamically. AES is recommended for encryption, and WEP is not used.
diffEn: Whereas the pre-shared key (PSK) method connects with a common password, the enterprise 802.1X / EAP method authenticates per user or endpoint. In exchange, operating the authentication server and certificates is required.
aiEn: Because the entrance of the internal Wi-Fi can be narrowed by authentication per user or endpoint, it is a foundation for limiting the endpoints that reach AI services and internal data to managed ones.

defEn: A cloud-based proxy for safely performing Web access to the outside and the like. It checks and evaluates safety from the destination URL or IP address, and blocks access if it evaluates it as unsafe.
howEn: It provides Web filtering, DNS filtering, DLP, malware detection, intrusion prevention, sandboxing and so on in a cloud form (IPA). Microsoft Entra Internet Access, a product example, links the context of user, device, location and risk with Conditional Access, and controls Web access based on identity.
diffEn: In the past, traffic had to go through the VPN gateway and the internal LAN before going out. With SWG, that function can be moved to the cloud. Whereas CASB narrows to visibility and data control for SaaS use, SWG handles Web access in general.
aiEn: Microsoft Entra Internet Access, a product example, lists shadow AI detection, prompt injection protection and DLP among its features. It becomes a means of controlling Web access to generative AI at the entrance.

defEn: A mechanism that places a single control point between users and multiple SaaS and the like, to visualize and control cloud use. It handles visibility into SaaS usage, access control, control of data exfiltration, threat detection and so on.
howEn: IPA organizes it with 4 elements: visibility, data security, compliance and threat protection. Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, a product example, identifies the SaaS in use from network traffic and the app catalog, evaluates risk with 90 or more indicators, and monitors continuously with policies.
diffEn: Whereas SWG handles safety checking and blocking of Web access in general, CASB narrows to SaaS use, visualizing it and controlling access and data exfiltration.
aiEn: Unapproved generative AI services, as a kind of SaaS, can also be made targets of discovery of use, risk evaluation and usage control. Control of exfiltration per data type also relates to operations that do not hand sensitive information to AI.

defEn: A method that, in place of VPN, which tends to reach a wide range, looks at identity and context (such as device state and risk) to permit connections finely per app. Based on the idea of Zero Trust, it always verifies.
howEn: In Microsoft's example, when a user requests a connection to an app, Entra ID single sign-on and Conditional Access are evaluated at the edge, and only approved apps are visible to the user. Decisions are made from signals of device state and risk, and when a risk is detected, continuous access evaluation re-evaluates or disconnects.
diffEn: VPN tends to reach a wide network after connecting. Microsoft presents a phased migration that starts from Quick Access, which grants broad access equivalent to VPN, and moves from important apps to per-app connections.
aiEn: It is a means of narrowing, per app and based on identity, remote access to generative AI apps that connect to internal data and to the management consoles of AI platforms.

defEn: Firewall functionality provided as a cloud service. It can protect with the same security settings communications from outside sites such as remote and mobile, communications between contracted cloud services and the outside, and even communications from personally owned devices (BYOD).
howEn: Communications are gathered at the cloud edge and inspected with the same policy. In Microsoft's classification, FWaaS is listed as an SSE function alongside SWG and CASB, and TLS inspection, URL filtering, DLP, threat intelligence and so on are applied at the edge.
diffEn: With a physical firewall appliance, the configuration of network rules and the control based on them are done on the same device. FWaaS places that function in the cloud, so it is not tied to an installation location.
aiEn: It is an option when you want to apply the same rules to communications to generative AI services regardless of site, home or mobile. It also serves as material for considering a design that consolidates and controls the egress.

defEn: Short for Software-Defined WAN. A function that controls wide area networks between sites and to the cloud by software, achieving flexible network configuration and traffic control and so on.
howEn: Devices on the site side (SD-WAN CPE) handle optimizing and selecting routes, and connect sites to cloud hubs with IPsec and the like. Microsoft's Azure Virtual WAN is itself a cloud-based SD-WAN, and also assumes interconnection with site-side SD-WAN and SASE.
diffEn: SASE is a framework that provides security functions such as CASB and SWG together with network functions such as SD-WAN from the cloud, and SD-WAN is positioned on its network side.
aiEn: It is a foundation for centrally controlling the routes to generative AI platforms and business systems distributed across sites, data centers and the cloud.

defEn: A new category of network security that points to a cloud-delivered, identity-aware network perimeter, which becomes necessary as places of work become distributed and apps and data move to the cloud. It includes SWG, CASB, FWaaS and so on.
howEn: In Microsoft's example, SSE is configured by combining Entra Internet Access (an identity-based SWG), which protects the Internet and SaaS, and Entra Private Access (ZTNA), which handles connections to internal resources, with Defender for Cloud Apps, a CASB. It is delivered from the edge of Microsoft's wide area network.
diffEn: SSE refers to the security functions side. SASE is a framework that also includes network functions such as SD-WAN, and Microsoft explains it as incorporating SSE's functions into the SASE framework.
aiEn: Global Secure Access, a product example, lists for the Internet detection of generative AI app use (shadow AI), prompt injection protection and DLP among its functions. This leads to the idea of concentrating control of AI use at the network entrance.

defEn: A framework that consolidates security and network technologies into a single cloud platform, enabling a safe and rapid move to the cloud (Gartner's definition, as introduced by IPA). Users use systems via SASE regardless of location.
howEn: Before communications enter SaaS or IaaS, security measures are applied with CASB, SDP, SWG and so on, and the network functions for the WAN and the Internet (CDN, SD-WAN and so on) are also provided from the cloud. In Microsoft's classification, communications are gathered at the edge and TLS inspection, URL filtering, DLP and so on are applied.
diffEn: Zero Trust is the idea of “not trusting implicitly”, and SASE is a framework that bundles functions in the cloud; Microsoft explains the two in combination. SSE refers to the security functions side of SASE.
aiEn: To control communications to generative AI, the configuration needs to route those communications through SASE. IPA's verification showed the finding that communications that do not pass through SASE cannot be detected.

defEn: A state in which hardware, software, cloud services and the like that have not been permitted are used without authorization. Security control by administrators can no longer be performed, and the risk of leakage of the business information that should be protected increases.
howEn: Identify the apps in use, assess their risk, and manage them by sorting them into approved and unapproved. In the Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps example, use is discovered through integration with Defender for Endpoint and collection of firewall and proxy logs, and unapproved apps are blocked with the firewall, proxy or SWG.
diffEn: Shadow AI is unauthorized use limited to generative AI apps and tools, and its main risks are data leakage to AI and compliance violations. Shadow IT refers to IT services in general, and its main risk is the dispersal of data.
aiEn: Shadow AI detection finds communications to ChatGPT, Claude and the like by network traffic analysis, and visualizes users, traffic volume and risk scores (Global Secure Access example). Proceed not only by prohibition but together with preparing approved alternatives.

defEn: A technology that separates Web browsing from the user's endpoint, runs it in a browser in an isolated environment such as the cloud, and sends only the rendered result to the endpoint. It is introduced to protect endpoints from phishing and attacks via the browser.
howEn: Page rendering and JavaScript execution are carried out by the browser in the isolated environment, and only an image of the screen (pixel stream) reaches the endpoint. Keystrokes and clicks are forwarded to the isolated side. Normally, all Web traffic is routed through the isolation platform by a proxy, and egress to the outside is restricted.
diffEn: Whereas SWG inspects communications and decides to allow or block, RBI does not run malicious code on the endpoint. By execution location, there are the cloud type, the on-premises type, and a local type that uses a container or virtual machine within the endpoint.
aiEn: In scenarios where you browse external links or unknown sites suggested by AI, it is a means of not letting the endpoint execute code. Because the flow of information in and out via the video remains, it needs to be used together with DLP and the like.

defEn: A mechanism that continuously evaluates the settings of SaaS apps, finds security deficiencies and misconfigurations, and shows the steps for improvement. It is posture management aimed at SaaS, and is abbreviated SSPM.
howEn: When a SaaS is connected with a connector, the evaluation results of its settings are shown as recommendations and can be checked in Secure Score. Microsoft Defender for Cloud Apps, a product example, organizes recommendations from multiple perspectives such as the CIS Microsoft 365 Foundations Benchmark, and also visualizes attack paths of OAuth apps.
diffEn: Whereas CASB monitors and controls the use and operation of SaaS, SSPM evaluates the safety of the settings of each SaaS themselves. It applies to SaaS an idea close to CSPM, which looks at the settings of cloud infrastructure.
aiEn: The generative AI features built into SaaS, and the settings of the privileges granted through external app integrations, can also be made targets of continuous inspection.

fullEn: API gateway / API security (authentication, authorization and control at the entrance of an API)
defEn: An entrance placed between the users of an API and the backend, which applies authentication and authorization, request validation, rate limiting and so on together. An API is the input/output window that one piece of software exposes to another.
howEn: The gateway validates JWTs and lets through only callers that hold a valid token. It validates the format of requests, and protects the backend with rate limits and quotas. mTLS with client certificates and IP restrictions can also be used. Subscription keys are not relied on as a means of authentication.
diffEn: Whereas a WAF inspects attack patterns against Web apps, an API gateway centers on authentication and authorization of the caller and control of usage volume. A configuration that places a WAF in front of the gateway is recommended.
aiEn: With a gateway for AI, you can authenticate with a managed identity so that API keys are unnecessary, set upper limits on token usage, and capture logs of prompts and responses (Azure API Management example).

fullEn: Local breakout (communication paths going directly from a site or endpoint to the Internet)
defEn: A configuration in which Internet-bound traffic from sites and teleworking endpoints is sent directly to the Internet from an exit close to the user, instead of being gathered at a central site such as headquarters. It is adopted to reduce latency of SaaS use and load on the internal line.
howEn: In the past, communications were gathered at headquarters, inspected, and sent out through a proxy. With local breakout, traffic goes straight out from the user's location to the nearest entry point, and DNS name resolution is also done nearby (Microsoft 365 example). What does not pass through central inspection is made up for by measures on the endpoint side and the cloud side.
diffEn: A configuration that returns traffic to headquarters by VPN can consolidate inspection, but latency increases. Local breakout keeps latency down but disperses the position of inspection, so it becomes a design that is supplemented with SWG, CASB and the like.
aiEn: For communications to generative AI services too, latency and the position of inspection change depending on whether they go via headquarters or a local exit. Decide where to apply inspection and DLP together with the design of the exit.

fullEn: CASB deployment modes (API connector / reverse proxy)
defEn: The difference in connection methods when CASB visualizes and controls SaaS. The representative ones are the API integration type, which connects to the SaaS's API, and the reverse proxy type, which routes the user's communications through it, and they are used in combination.
howEn: The API integration type (app connector) gains visibility and control through the SaaS provider's API, but because of API limits, scanning all files can take several hours to several days. The reverse proxy type routes communications in coordination with conditional access and performs actions such as blocking downloads during the session.
diffEn: The API type centers on understanding the state and operations of connected SaaS, and the proxy type centers on immediate control during a session. The proxy type targets browser operations, and native clients may be out of scope.
aiEn: SaaS-type generative AI can also have its settings and sharing status checked if it can be connected by API. For browser use, session control such as blocking uploads can be considered. Check whether it is supported for each product.

fullEn: Enterprise / secure browser (building controls into the browser used for work)
defEn: An approach that builds security controls into the browser used for work and manages operations such as uploading, copying and printing. Its distinguishing feature is that control takes place inside the browser, without routing traffic through a separate proxy.
howEn: In the product example, Microsoft Edge for Business monitors and blocks downloads, uploads, copy and paste, and printing inside the browser, in sessions that use the work profile. In the Chrome Enterprise example, features include binding session Cookies to the device and enforcing the download save location.
diffEn: RBI moves the place where browsing is executed into an isolated environment, whereas a secure browser puts the controls into the browser on the user's own device. Microsoft explains that, compared with a reverse proxy, it avoids latency and application compatibility problems.
aiEn: Even on BYOD and contractors' devices, downloading and pasting of data can be controlled inside the browser. In some situations it can be used as a measure against data being taken out to AI services used in the browser.

fullEn: Tenant restrictions (restricting the use of accounts from external tenants)
defEn: A mechanism that restricts signing in to SaaS with accounts of external organisations or individuals from the organisation's own network or devices. Only the external tenants to be allowed are specified, and all others are denied by default.
howEn: In the Microsoft Entra ID example, cross-tenant access settings block external accounts and external apps by default, and only the tenants to be allowed, such as business partners, are made exceptions. A proxy, Global Secure Access or a Windows policy adds a header to the request, and Entra ID enforces the restriction.
diffEn: Whereas restriction by fixed IP narrows the connection sources on the SaaS side, tenant restrictions narrow which tenants' accounts can be used to sign in from the organisation's own devices and networks.
aiEn: It can narrow the routes by which employees reach SaaS from the work environment using personal or external-organisation accounts. What can be controlled is limited to the range of identities supported.

defEn: A concept showing how security responsibilities are divided between the cloud provider and the customer. The division changes depending on whether IaaS, PaaS or SaaS is used, and data and identities always remain the customer's responsibility.
howEn: In Microsoft's breakdown, data, configuration, and identities and users are the customer's responsibility in every deployment type. Physical hosts, the physical network and the datacentre become the provider's responsibility from IaaS onwards. The OS, network controls and applications are shared with the provider depending on the type.
diffEn: Google describes a shift away from merely drawing a line of responsibility, towards “shared fate”, in which the provider supplies extensive guidance and tools.
aiEn: Microsoft extends this to generative AI and organises it into three layers: the AI platform, the AI application and AI usage. In the usage layer, updating usage policies and providing training are the customer's duties.

defEn: A mechanism that continuously inspects the configuration of cloud resources, finds misconfigurations and weaknesses that violate security policy, and presents them as recommendations for improvement. It keeps resources in the cloud in a secure state (posture).
howEn: The policies that have been defined are converted into recommendations that point to violating settings, and the secure score rises as remediation progresses. It can also connect to multicloud environments, and attack path analysis lets you check risky routes as well (example: Microsoft Defender for Cloud).
diffEn: Whereas CWPP protects running workloads from threats, CSPM centres on checking configuration and posture. CNAPP is what bundles the two.
aiEn: AI SPM in Defender for Cloud detects generative AI workloads, presents an AI BOM and assesses their posture.

defEn: A mechanism that protects workloads running in the cloud, such as virtual machines, containers, storage, databases and serverless functions, from threats. It provides workload-specific recommendations and alerts.
howEn: Per-workload recommendations indicate the controls that are needed, and when a threat is detected an alert reports its nature and severity. In the example, it provides vulnerability assessment and file integrity monitoring for servers, environment hardening and runtime protection for containers, and malware scanning for storage.
diffEn: Whereas CSPM checks that settings are correct, CWPP handles threat detection and defence for running workloads. CNAPP integrates the two.
aiEn: The AI Services plan of Defender for Cloud identifies threats to generative AI applications in real time and helps with the response.

defEn: A platform that integrates multiple cloud security functions and protects applications in the cloud across the whole lifecycle from development to operation. It brings CSPM, CWPP and others together into a single experience.
howEn: Defender for Cloud places CSPM, DevSecOps and CWPP at its core. It links misconfigurations and exposed secrets at the code stage with the state of the cloud in order to prioritise remediation. Google explains that integration with security operations is advancing.
diffEn: Introducing CSPM and CWPP separately as single-function products increases the number of products. CNAPP is moving towards reducing the number of point products by integrating them.
aiEn: Defender for Cloud provides posture management and threat protection for generative AI workloads. Google's SCC Enterprise also lists preventive and detective controls for AI workloads.

defEn: A mechanism that identifies the permissions granted to identities in the cloud, such as people, apps and service accounts, finds excessive, unused and misconfigured permissions, and brings them closer to the principle of least privilege. It looks across multiple clouds.
howEn: For example, Microsoft Defender for Cloud tracks permissions across Azure, AWS and GCP on a single screen and, from effective permissions, identifies the identities that can reach sensitive resources. It recommends removing dormant accounts, limiting administrator permissions and right-sizing permissions based on actual usage, and also shows lateral movement from over-privileged identities as an attack path.
diffEn: IAM is itself the mechanism that grants and manages permissions, whereas CIEM inspects, across multiple clouds, whether permissions that have already been granted are excessive. There are examples where it is provided as a function of CSPM.
aiEn: It covers not only users but also non-human identities such as service principals, managed identities and service accounts. It can also be used to review the permissions of identities used by AI agents and inference platforms.

defEn: A mechanism for connecting to cloud PaaS services, and to services provided by other companies, through a private address inside your own virtual network, without going over the public internet.
howEn: In Azure Private Link, for example, a private endpoint is created inside the virtual network, and traffic to storage or SQL Database travels over Microsoft's backbone network. Because an endpoint corresponds to a specific resource rather than to the whole service, and connections to other resources are blocked, the risk of data exfiltration is reduced.
diffEn: Whereas a VPN sets up an encrypted tunnel between networks, Private Link places the access point to a specific cloud service inside your own network. From on-premises it can be used via VPN or ExpressRoute.
aiEn: It is a way to separate traffic to generative AI services and AI data stores from the public internet and limit it to connections from the internal network.

fullEn: Infrastructure as Code Security (security of infrastructure configuration defined in code)
defEn: For IaC, which defines cloud configuration in code (templates), the practice of inspecting the code before deployment to find misconfigurations and keep insecure configurations from reaching the production environment. Problems can be fixed at an early stage of development.
howEn: Templates such as ARM, Bicep, Terraform and CloudFormation are statically inspected in the repository or the pipeline. Microsoft Security DevOps uses Template Analyzer, Checkov and Terrascan, can be run from GitHub Actions or an Azure DevOps extension, and lets you review the results in Defender for Cloud.
diffEn: Whereas CSPM checks the settings of running cloud resources, IaC security checks templates before deployment to prevent misconfigurations from entering production.
aiEn: If the network, permissions and storage of an AI platform are also built with IaC, errors in exposure settings and permissions can be checked at the code stage.

defEn: An approach for cloud-native environments that protects container images, registries, Kubernetes clusters, nodes and running workloads from three angles: configuration weaknesses, vulnerabilities and runtime threats.
howEn: For example, Microsoft Defender for Containers performs continuous monitoring of configuration, vulnerability assessment of images in registries and of running containers, and runtime threat detection for clusters, nodes and workloads. Policies such as gated deployment, which audits or rejects the deployment of vulnerable images, and a ban on creating privileged containers can also be used.
diffEn: Unlike traditional protection centred on the host (VM), it treats image vulnerabilities, cluster API settings and runtime behaviour inside containers as separate layers.
aiEn: When generative AI inference platforms or agents are run on Kubernetes, too, scanning images for vulnerabilities and prohibiting unnecessary privileges are the starting point.

fullEn: DevSecOps and CI/CD Pipeline Security (building security into development and operations, and protecting the build and deployment infrastructure)
defEn: A concept and practice with two aspects: automatically building security checks into the pipeline from development to deployment (shift left), and at the same time protecting the build and deployment infrastructure itself from attack. Vulnerabilities and misconfigurations are found at an early stage.
howEn: For example, the Microsoft cloud security benchmark shows building SAST, secret scanning, IaC scanning and DAST into CI/CD, and managing secrets centrally in places such as Key Vault. Permissions to change the pipeline are restricted, images are inspected before deployment, and DevOps audit logs are aggregated to detect unauthorised changes.
diffEn: Unlike the traditional approach of inspecting at the final stage, it embeds inspection and continuous monitoring in every stage. Not only the application code but also the pipeline's credentials and approval mechanisms are covered by protection.
aiEn: Because deployment of AI apps also goes through the same pipeline, a takeover of the pipeline can lead to tampering with the AI app as a whole.

fullEn: Landing Zone and Guardrails (a cloud adoption foundation, and automated rules that prevent and detect deviations)
defEn: A concept combining the common foundation prepared before an organisation starts using the cloud (the landing zone) with the automated rules on top of it that prevent and detect deviations from the rules (guardrails). It reconciles delegating authority to teams on the front line with maintaining control.
howEn: In Azure, for example, policies are assigned at levels of the hierarchy such as management groups and subscriptions, and are inherited by everything beneath. You can choose effects such as rejecting non-compliant changes, only logging them, or automatically deploying related settings. It is recommended to start with audit, confirm the impact, and then move to enforcement.
diffEn: Whereas RBAC decides who is allowed to perform operations, policy evaluates whether the state of a resource conforms to the rules. Even with permission, creation or updating is denied if it is non-compliant.
aiEn: If restricting allowed regions and making it mandatory to send diagnostic logs are applied to a subscription for AI, a minimum level of control is maintained even when teams on the front line create new AI environments.

nameEn: SBOM and software supply chain management
fullEn: Software Bill of Materials / Software Supply Chain Security
defEn: An effort to prepare a list (SBOM) recording the components that make up software and their supply relationships, manage the vulnerabilities and provenance of dependencies, and reduce the risk of attacks and contamination via the supply chain.
howEn: NIST describes an SBOM as a formal record of the details of the components used to build software and their supply relationships, and lists SPDX, CycloneDX and SWID as standard formats. The Microsoft benchmark shows maintaining a list of direct and transitive dependencies, continuously checking it against new CVEs, and preventing the introduction of risky dependencies.
diffEn: An SBOM is a list of components and does not guarantee that the software was built securely. NIST positions it as complementing, not replacing, vulnerability management and vendor risk assessment.
aiEn: It can be used to understand the libraries and container images that an AI app depends on. It is also a perspective for requesting component information on AI-related software introduced from outside at the time of procurement.

defEn: An effort to protect public and internal APIs through authentication and authorisation, usage limits, input validation, narrowing of exposure and inventory management. The OWASP API Security Top 10 is used to organise threats.
howEn: At a gateway such as Azure API Management, for example, OAuth 2 token validation, rate limits and quotas, schema-based validation of requests and responses, and rejection of undefined endpoints are enforced in one place. Managed identities are used for backend authentication, and the list of APIs and their versions is also managed.
diffEn: Whereas a WAF protects against traditional Web attacks and bots, API security centres on controls that follow the API's specification, such as object-level authorisation and usage limits. The two complement each other.
aiEn: For APIs for generative AI, usage and cost can be managed by setting an upper limit on the number of tokens (token limit) and by emitting consumption metrics.

defEn: A mechanism that prevents sensitive information such as credit card numbers and medical records from leaking to, or being shared with, unauthorised parties. It identifies and monitors sensitive information based on policy and automatically applies protection to inappropriate operations.
