howEn: Policy defines the locations and conditions to cover, and content is analysed using keywords, regular expressions, machine learning and so on. When there is a match, actions such as showing a warning, blocking sharing and quarantining are carried out, and the operation is recorded in the audit log (example: Microsoft Purview).
diffEn: Data classification and sensitivity labels are a mechanism for attaching a mark that indicates sensitivity, and DLP controls sharing and taking data out using those marks or the content as conditions. The two are used in combination.
aiEn: Purview DLP includes Microsoft 365 Copilot among the locations it monitors, and can also cover the sending of sensitive information to ChatGPT, Gemini, DeepSeek and others via the browser or the network.

fullEn: Key Management Service / Hardware Security Module
defEn: Key management (KMS) centrally manages the creation, storage and usage permissions of the keys that encrypt data. An HSM is a device that protects keys inside dedicated hardware, and in the cloud it is also provided as a service.
howEn: In the cloud, you can choose between keys managed by the provider and customer-managed keys that the customer creates and manages. Key encryption keys protect other encryption keys, and protection levels are provided in steps, from software-protected key management to single-tenant HSMs (example: Azure).
diffEn: Whereas the standard key management service protects keys in software, the HSM type protects keys inside certified hardware. With the single-tenant type, the customer holds the root of trust for the keys.
aiEn: Customer-managed keys can be used for encryption at rest even on the platform that holds in-house data to be passed to generative AI. Whether to hold the keys in-house is a point to be decided from regulatory and contractual requirements.

defEn: An effort to divide information into categories according to its sensitivity (public, company confidential and so on) and assign them as labels. Protections such as encryption, watermarks and sharing restrictions can be applied according to the label, and the label stays with the information.
howEn: Administrators create categories that suit the organisation (example: Public, General, Confidential, Highly Confidential), and labels are applied by user action or by automatic detection. The label is stored in the file's metadata and stays with it even when the storage location changes (example: Microsoft Purview).
diffEn: DLP is the side that stops sharing and taking data out using labels or content as conditions, while the label indicates sensitivity and serves as the starting point for protection. Retention labels are for controlling the retention period and are applied separately from sensitivity labels.
aiEn: Microsoft 365 Copilot and agents recognise sensitivity labels. For labels that involve encryption, they return only data from items for which the user has the copy permission (EXTRACT).

fullEn: Immutable Backup (backup that cannot be deleted or altered)
defEn: A backup protected so that it can be neither deleted nor altered during its retention period. Even if ransomware or a malicious operation tries to wipe out the backups themselves, the recovery points used for recovery can be preserved.
howEn: The immutable vault of Azure Backup prohibits operations that would lead to the loss of recovery points (deletion before expiry, shortening the retention period), and, once it is locked, it can no longer be disabled (WORM storage). The Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications lists the combined use of physical isolation, automatic encryption and network isolation.
diffEn: With an ordinary backup, anyone with the permission can delete recovery points. An immutable setting differs in that it cannot be disabled after it is locked. Recovery drills are also needed separately.
aiEn: Internal data that grows with the introduction of generative AI (such as documents and indexes for search) should also be included in the scope of backups, with the recovery targets and retention periods decided.

defEn: A mechanism that automatically discovers data stores across multiple clouds, grasps where sensitive data is located, who has access to it and how it is protected, and continuously finds and prioritises risks that could lead to data exfiltration.
howEn: For example, Defender for Cloud discovers object stores and databases across multiple clouds and samples the data to determine the types of sensitive information. It assesses data exposure and data flows, and also shows attack paths from internet-exposed VMs to sensitive data. DSPM in Purview answers what data exists where, who can access it and how it is protected.
diffEn: Whereas DLP detects and blocks operations that take data out, DSPM is the area that finds where sensitive data is located and the gaps in its protection. It differs from CSPM in that it starts from the data itself rather than from infrastructure or devices.
aiEn: DSPM in Purview makes the activity of AI apps and agents visible and tracks interactions that contain sensitive data and excessive sharing.

defEn: A technique that handles sensitive values such as credit card numbers by replacing them with meaningless substitute values (tokens). If the substitute value has the same character type and length, it can also fit the format constraints of existing systems.
howEn: For example, Cloud DLP in Google Cloud replaces input values with tokens of the same character type and length using format-preserving encryption (FPE), keeping compatibility with legacy systems that have format constraints. A prefix indicating that the value can be restored can also be added. There is also a method that replaces values with a one-way hash generated with a key; in this case the original cannot be recovered.
diffEn: Whereas masking hides some characters with fixed characters, tokenization replaces the entire value with a substitute value. It can be stored and processed while preserving the format, and depending on the method the original can also be restored.
aiEn: If personal information and account numbers are replaced with tokens before being passed to generative AI, processing can proceed without sending the raw values to the model or external services.

defEn: A technique that hides part or all of sensitive data with masking characters or other values so that unauthorised users, and people in development and testing, do not see the real data as it is. There are methods that hide it dynamically, only at display time, and methods that process and replace the values.
howEn: Dynamic masking does not change the values stored in the database and hides only the query results for unauthorised users (example: Azure SQL Database). Rules define the target columns and functions; for credit cards only the last 4 digits are shown, and for email only the first character. Users with the UNMASK permission, and administrators, can see the original values.
diffEn: Dynamic masking does not change the stored values and controls only how results are displayed. It differs in its handling of the original data from tokenization, which replaces the entire value with a substitute value.
aiEn: In AI testing and fault investigation that use production data, showing developers only the masked results can limit the exposure of personal information.

nameEn: Pseudonymously processed information and anonymously processed information
fullEn: Pseudonymously / Anonymously Processed Information (processed information under the Act on the Protection of Personal Information)
defEn: Categories under the Act on the Protection of Personal Information. Pseudonymously processed information is information processed so that an individual cannot be identified unless it is compared with other information (Article 2, paragraph 5); anonymously processed information is information processed so that an individual cannot be identified and the original cannot be restored (the same Article, paragraph 6).
howEn: Anonymously processed information does not constitute personal information and can be provided to third parties without the consent of the individual concerned. Pseudonymously processed information, because its creator normally retains the original information, is in principle personal information, and provision to third parties is in principle prohibited, but the purpose of use can be changed beyond the scope of relevance. The obligations at the time of creation are set out in the guidelines (Pseudonymously Processed Information and Anonymously Processed Information volume).
diffEn: Whereas anonymously processed information cannot be restored and is not personal information, pseudonymously processed information can be identified if compared with other information and is in principle personal information. Masking and tokenization are technical methods, not legal categories.
aiEn: Before using data that contains personal information for AI analysis or training, consider which kind of processed information it can be handled as. The treatment of provision to third parties and of the purpose of use changes depending on the category.

fullEn: Data Residency and Cross-Border Data Transfer
defEn: The geographic location where data is stored and processed (data residency), and the regulation of data movement across national borders. Japan's Act on the Protection of Personal Information sets rules for providing personal data to a third party in a foreign country (Article 28).
howEn: As a rule, the consent of the individual concerned to the provision to a foreign country must be obtained in advance. Consent is not required where the destination country is specified in rules as a country with a system of an equivalent standard, or where the recipient has put in place a system that conforms to the standards. When obtaining consent, the name of the destination country, the system of that country and the measures taken by the recipient are presented to the individual. For provision based on a standards-conforming system, the status of implementation must be checked at least about once a year.
diffEn: Data residency is a choice of where to place data (in the cloud, chosen by region), whereas cross-border transfer regulation is the legal discipline imposed on provision to third parties in foreign countries. Both need to be checked.
aiEn: When passing personal data to a generative AI service that runs in an overseas region, check whether this amounts to provision to a third party in a foreign country or to outsourcing. Outsourcing is likewise treated as subject to Article 28.

defEn: Processing, erasing and disposing of storage media and data that are no longer needed, to the point where access to the target data is infeasible with a given level of effort. NIST calls this processing media sanitization.
howEn: NIST SP 800-88 provides guidance for sanitization plans that determine the erasure and disposal techniques and controls according to the sensitivity of the information. For example, after data upload is complete, Azure Data Box performs a block-level erase of the data on the device, and a certificate of erasure in line with NIST SP 800-88 can be obtained from the portal.
diffEn: Whereas data retention determines how long data is kept, data erasure and disposal is the final step that, after the period has expired, reliably makes the target inaccessible.
aiEn: Data copied for AI training and testing, and data inside environments that are no longer in use, are also covered. Data cannot be erased unless the locations of the copies are known.

nameEn: Encryption at rest and in transit
fullEn: Encryption at Rest / in Transit (encryption of stored data and encryption of communications)
defEn: Encryption at rest, which protects stored data, and encryption in transit, which protects data flowing over a network. They are sometimes organised into three states by adding encryption in use, which protects data while it is being processed.
howEn: For example, Azure uses server-side encryption with AES-256 at rest, and key models such as service-managed keys and customer-managed keys can be chosen. In transit, data is protected with TLS, and Azure is moving towards TLS 1.2 or later. VPNs are encrypted with IPsec. Confidential computing is used for encryption in use.
diffEn: This is a different axis from key management (KMS, HSM), which deals with who manages keys and where; this one is a classification of which state of data is being protected. The two are used in combination.
aiEn: Encryption is needed both on the communication path used to pass data to generative AI and at the storage location of the data placed for RAG. For data being processed, confidential computing is an option.

fullEn: Data Retention and Lifecycle Management (retention policies and retention labels)
defEn: Setting and operating rules to keep data for a fixed period in accordance with laws and internal regulations and to delete it after that period. What must be kept is reliably kept, and old information that is no longer needed is deleted to reduce risk.
howEn: For example, Microsoft Purview combines two operations, retain (prevent deletion and keep the data available to eDiscovery) and delete, and can be set to retain only, delete only, or retain and then delete. There are retention policies at the level of sites and mailboxes, and retention labels at the level of documents and emails, and a disposition review can be inserted when the period expires.
diffEn: Whereas an immutable backup protects copies used for recovery from failures and attacks, data retention keeps the original content for legal and regulatory purposes and deletes it after the deadline.
aiEn: Interactions with Copilot and AI apps can also be included in the scope of a retention policy. This provides a basis for deciding the retention period of prompts and responses in line with internal regulations.

defEn: A mechanism that encrypts files and emails and attaches usage permissions such as viewing, editing, printing and forwarding to the data itself, so that protection continues even after the data moves to sharing recipients, outside the company, or to unmanaged storage. Rights management is carried by the data.
howEn: For example, Azure Rights Management protects files and emails with encryption, identity and authorisation policies. Encryption settings can be applied through sensitivity labels, and protection remains even if a file moves to unmanaged storage. “Do Not Forward” restricts forwarding, printing and copying. Auditing of usage and revoking access to Office files are also possible.
diffEn: Whereas DLP detects and blocks taking data out by means of policy, IRM attaches protection to the data itself. However, sharing such as screen capture cannot be completely prevented, and it is assumed to be used together with other controls.
aiEn: Material encrypted with a sensitivity label cannot be read even if it reaches an unauthorised party. Before using internal documents as a reference source for generative AI, it is a point to check whether they are handled with protection still attached.

fullEn: Electronic Discovery and Legal Hold (electronic evidence disclosure and litigation hold)
defEn: A procedure for identifying electronically stored information that may become evidence in an investigation or litigation, preserving and collecting it, and putting it in a state where it can be produced. The measure that stops deletion of the target data for preservation is a legal hold.
howEn: For example, Microsoft Purview eDiscovery manages search, hold and export on a per-case basis. A hold is placed on target locations such as email, Teams and SharePoint to prevent deletion, and search results are collected into a review set, tagged and analysed before being exported.
diffEn: Whereas data retention sets periods by company-wide rules, a legal hold is a case-by-case measure that preserves targets for a specific investigation or litigation.
aiEn: eDiscovery also supports searching and deleting Copilot and AI app data. In preparation for cases where interactions with AI become subject to discovery, decide the policy for retention and preservation in advance.

defEn: A security platform that aggregates and analyses logs and events from across networks, devices, the cloud, applications and other sources, and is used for threat detection, incident investigation and compliance.
howEn: Logs are collected with agents or connectors and normalised into a common format. Correlation rules and machine learning link related events to find anomalies, and prioritised alerts according to severity are raised. Analysts investigate using search and visualisation.
diffEn: The SOC is the people and team who use a SIEM, and SOAR is a mechanism for automating response after detection. SIEM is the technical platform responsible for collecting, analysing and detecting data.
aiEn: In Google's explanation, machine learning models are used for detection in SIEM. If logs of generative AI use are also ingested, they can be correlated with logs from other systems on the same platform to investigate suspicious use.

defEn: A mechanism that links multiple security tools (orchestration), automates routine alert-handling tasks (automation), and speeds up the process from detection to response.
howEn: Depending on conditions, predefined response procedures (playbooks) are run automatically or manually. As an example, when malware is detected on a device, isolation, evidence collection, searching other systems for similar indicators and ticket creation are carried out automatically, and the case is passed on for confirmation by the person in charge.
diffEn: Whereas SIEM handles collection, analysis and detection, SOAR coordinates and automates the response after detection. SOAR is used alongside SIEM, in the form of automating the response to threats that SIEM has detected.
aiEn: In a SOC with many alerts, it automates routine investigation and response so that people can concentrate on investigating advanced threats. Alerts related to generative AI can also be put through the same procedures.

defEn: A team or organisation in which security specialists monitor information systems and carry out threat detection, investigation and response. It uses technical platforms such as SIEM as its main tools and analyses signs of attack.
howEn: It analyses logs and alerts to investigate suspicious access and takes action as necessary. The Digital Agency's policy cites an approach in which, when suspicious access is recognised, the organisation responds jointly with SOCs inside and outside the organisation, and both sides monitor through log integration and shared dashboards.
diffEn: SIEM is a tool that a SOC uses. The glossary of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications explains a CSIRT as a structure for monitoring and analysis of causes, so the roles of a SOC and a CSIRT overlap.
aiEn: Add the usage logs and control status of generative AI apps to what is monitored, and build the handling of alerts into operating procedures. Whether to operate it in-house or outsource it is also a decision point.

defEn: An effort to acquire and store records of communications and operations (audit logs) from firewalls, authentication, servers, applications and so on, and to use them for early detection of incidents, investigation of causes, investigation of the scope of impact, and consideration of measures to prevent recurrence.
howEn: The types of logs to acquire and their retention periods are decided from the data handled and the attacks anticipated. Time is synchronised with NTP, and logs are stored in a log management system separate from the devices to prevent tampering. Because logs may contain personal information and the like, they are treated as confidential information.
diffEn: SIEM includes log management at its core while also handling correlation analysis, detection and response. Log management is the foundation of acquisition, storage and search, and SIEM layers detection on top of it.
aiEn: For generative AI use as well, logs that make it possible to trace who handled which data and when are needed for investigation and audit. Decide in advance what is acquired, the retention period, and how confidential information inside logs is handled.

defEn: The series of processes in which an organisation makes security decisions based on intelligence obtained by collecting, processing and analysing threat information about cyberattacks. It is not a term that refers to a specific tool or service.
howEn: It runs in a cycle of policy setting, collection and processing, analysis, dissemination and evaluation. By user, it is organised into three types (IPA): strategic, for executive management; operational, used to understand attack methods and for penetration testing; and tactical, such as IoCs for the SOC.
diffEn: IoCs such as malicious IPs and hash values are one kind of tactical intelligence and are only a part of threat intelligence. IPA also cites use at the strategic and operational levels as an issue.
aiEn: Include trends in attacks targeting generative AI, and in its misuse, in threat information, and use them as material for judging the impact on your own organisation and the priority of responses.

defEn: A vulnerability assessment is work that comprehensively inspects the whole target system to identify weaknesses. A penetration test is an examination that attacks from the same viewpoint as an attacker and confirms, on a risk basis, whether the attack actually succeeds.
howEn: A vulnerability assessment covers servers, network devices, Web apps and Web APIs, smartphone apps and so on, and, measured against standards, also identifies points that do not immediately lead to an attack. A penetration test checks whether the objective can be achieved in an anticipated attack scenario and also confirms the extent of damage.
diffEn: An assessment centres on comprehensiveness; a penetration test centres on whether the attack succeeds and confirming the damage. The Digital Agency states that vulnerabilities that are hard to anticipate in an assessment need to be checked by testing from the attacker's viewpoint.
aiEn: Microsoft cloud security benchmark v2 (preview) lists, as controls, regular red team exercises and, in addition, continuous AI red teaming (AI-7).

defEn: A structure in companies and government agencies that monitors whether any problems are occurring in information systems and, when they do, analyses causes and investigates the scope of impact. Incident response refers to the response activities that proceed from the detection of an incident to recovery.
howEn: The flow of detection, initial response (contacting the relevant departments, preventing the spread of damage, providing information to security response organisations), analysis, recovery and prevention of recurrence is turned into procedures in advance. Because there are cases where delays in conveying information to senior management led to mistakes in the initial response, rules for communication are set in advance.
diffEn: In the glossary of the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, CERT is an organisation that carries out activities to respond to incidents, and is a name also used in handling international cooperation. CSIRT refers to a structure within an organisation and overlaps with the SOC in terms of monitoring.
aiEn: Incidents of information leakage or erroneous output by generative AI are also to be put on the existing response procedures. Decide in advance who makes the decisions, the contact points, and the criteria for escalating to senior management.

defEn: An analytical technique that learns the baseline of normal behaviour not only for users but also for entities such as hosts, IP addresses and applications, and detects deviations from it as anomalies.
howEn: Machine learning builds behavioural profiles, and current activity is compared with the subject's own past, with its peer group (peers determined dynamically from, for example, the group it belongs to) and with the organisation as a whole. Anomalies are given a risk score based on deviations in location, device and frequency, and the score is used to prioritise investigation.
diffEn: It is an analytics function that runs on top of a SIEM and is not the SIEM itself. As an example, Microsoft Sentinel has UEBA built in, and its results can be brought into investigation and hunting queries.
aiEn: Because applications are also treated as entities, the approach can be applied to detecting unusual behaviour of generative AI user accounts and integrated apps.

fullEn: Attack Surface Management / External Attack Surface Management
defEn: An activity that continuously discovers and inventories the organisation's own assets visible from the internet side (domains, IP addresses, hosts and so on) and grasps the weaknesses of the attack surface that extends outside the firewall.
howEn: Known legitimate assets are used as the starting points of discovery (seeds), and observable connections are followed to explore recursively domains, IP address blocks, hosts, email contacts, ASNs and so on. The assets found are classified and made into an inventory, and are examined from the perspective of vulnerabilities and security hygiene.
diffEn: Whereas a vulnerability assessment examines targets that have been decided in advance, ASM starts by following relationships from known assets to find assets that the IT department has not identified.
aiEn: It is a means of identifying externally exposed assets that the IT department is not aware of, such as test sites and public API entry points hurriedly put together for generative AI.

defEn: An activity in which analysts form hypotheses, search the data and verify those hypotheses to proactively look for undetected threats and malicious behaviour that have not appeared in alerts. The results are linked to new detections and investigations.
howEn: Hypotheses are formed from suspicious behaviour, new attack campaigns, gaps in detection and so on. Logs are examined with queries such as KQL, evidence is kept in bookmarks, and findings are reflected in new detection rules, threat intelligence and incidents. Results are measured by, for example, the number of validated hypotheses.
diffEn: Whereas SIEM detection rules react to known patterns, hunting looks for threats that have no alert. The insights gained are fed back into SIEM as detection rules.
aiEn: If logs such as authentication and API calls of generative AI and integrated apps are being collected, unusual usage patterns can be taken as hypotheses and investigated.

defEn: A science that supports criminal and civil proceedings through the recovery and investigation of digital data. The field that acquires and analyses data from computers, virtual machines and storage media is called computer forensics.
howEn: To withstand legal requirements, the chain of custody of evidence is maintained at each stage of acquisition, preservation and access. In the example, a snapshot of the disk is saved in immutable (WORM) storage, the hash value is recorded in a separate key vault, and access is logged.
diffEn: Whereas incident response (CSIRT) carries out containment and recovery, forensics takes on the aspect of preserving and analysing the acquired data as evidence.
aiEn: If logs of prompts and outputs are to be used as evidence in a generative-AI-related incident, the retention period, tamper prevention and restriction of who can view them need to be decided in advance.

defEn: A BCP is a plan for continuing business even when failures or disasters occur, and is based on risk assessment. DR is the part that plans recovery from rare and critical outages (natural disasters, serious human errors, ransomware, etc.).
howEn: Business functions are classified by importance, risks are identified and divided into those handled by high availability (HA) and those handled by DR, and mitigation measures are designed. For DR, the maximum tolerable period of data loss (RPO) and the maximum duration of downtime (RTO) are determined, procedure manuals are prepared, and they are verified through drills.
diffEn: HA is resilience to everyday temporary failures, whereas DR is the response to rare, critical outages. Backup is one means of DR, and restoring from it involves data loss and time.
aiEn: When a generative AI service has been built into business operations, decide in advance on falling back to manual work when that service stops, and on RTO and RPO according to the importance of the business function.

fullEn: MITRE ATT&CK (a knowledge base of attacker tactics and techniques)
defEn: A publicly available knowledge base that anyone can consult, compiling the tactics and techniques that attackers commonly use. It is created and maintained on the basis of real-world observations and is used for purposes such as building threat models.
howEn: Techniques are mapped to detection rules, hunting queries, bookmarks and incidents, and a matrix visualises which techniques have detections, revealing gaps in detection. In the example, Microsoft Sentinel aligns with version 18 of ATT&CK and displays active detections overlaid with those not yet configured.
diffEn: Whereas CIS Controls and NIST CSF organise the defender's measures and outcomes, ATT&CK organises from the side of attacker behaviour and is used for threat models and for checking detection.
aiEn: Even for attacks targeting generative AI and AI agents, mapping them to existing techniques such as credential theft and privilege escalation makes it possible to check for gaps in detection.

nameEn: Security awareness training and targeted-attack email drills
fullEn: Security Awareness Training / Phishing Simulation (training and simulated-email drills)
defEn: An effort combining training that teaches employees attack methods and correct responses with drills that send simulated attack emails to check whether they can respond appropriately on receiving a suspicious email; targeted-attack email drills are a representative example.
howEn: It is carried out after deciding the attack to be assumed, what is to be checked and the target people. Metrics include, besides the open rate, the rate of appropriate responses achieved, the time until a report reaches the responsible department, and whether there are any problems in the CSIRT's response flow. Recipients report to the internal responsible department, not to the sender. Some products also assign training according to the user's actions.
diffEn: Whereas a vulnerability assessment examines flaws in devices and systems, this checks whether people's responses and reporting routes work in an emergency. Drills that pose as a real organisation should be avoided.
aiEn: Include the rules for using generative AI (approved tools, information that may be entered) in the training content, and also check in drills the reporting route for when misuse is found.

fullEn: Zero Trust (the concept in NIST SP 800-207)
defEn: A concept in which implicit trust is not granted on the basis of network location or asset ownership alone, and access is permitted resource by resource after authentication and authorisation of the user and the device. It arose as a response to the growth of remote users, BYOD and cloud assets.
howEn: NIST shifts the focus of defence from static network perimeters to users, assets and resources. The Digital Agency sets out six application policies: identification of resources, identity proofing and user authentication, network protection, checking the state of resources, policy evaluation, and observation of resources and access.
diffEn: Perimeter-based defence assumes that the inside is trusted, and zero trust removes that assumption. The Digital Agency explains that zero trust does not negate perimeter-based or network measures, nor does it refer to a specific product.
aiEn: Access to generative AI services can also be made subject to permission after evaluating the state of the user and the device. Because zero trust is a concept rather than a product, it is advanced step by step.

defEn: The traditional concept that tries to block external attacks and internal information leakage by separating the inside from the outside at a boundary. It rests on the assumption that “untrusted things” do not enter the inside and that only “trusted things” exist inside.
howEn: A boundary is established using the network, and communications are controlled. A policy that permits only specific source and destination addresses and specific ports also falls under this concept. It centres on building a secure network, and the Digital Agency regards this as the basis of conventional security.
diffEn: Zero trust assumes that even the inside of the boundary can be compromised and evaluates resource by resource. The weakness of the perimeter-based approach is said to be that it is hard to stop free movement inside after an intrusion.
aiEn: Cloud generative AI services lie outside the internal boundary. The Digital Agency points out the risk that, as cloud use spreads, the perimeter-based approach alone will become insufficient.

defEn: NIST's framework that systematises outcomes for managing and reducing cybersecurity risk. It can be used regardless of industry or size, and many organisations use it voluntarily.
howEn: The Core consists of six Functions, Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond and Recover, which are run concurrently and continuously. Organisational Profiles describe the current state and the target, and priorities are set from the gap between them.
diffEn: The CSF only indicates the outcomes to be achieved and does not specify concrete actions. The means of realisation are supplemented by informative references to 50 or more documents, such as SP 800-53.
aiEn: NIST says it currently has no plans to update the CSF Core for AI, while explaining that existing outcomes can be used, such as monitoring the risks of third-party AI tools (GV.SC-07) and taking inventory of software including AI (ID.AM-02).

defEn: The mechanism by which an organisation operates and manages information security (information security management system). It is standardised as the international standard ISO/IEC 27001, and the standard defines the requirements for an ISMS.
howEn: In addition to requirements, the standard presents a list of controls for managing information risk, but does not make any specific control mandatory. An organisation obtains certification by undergoing assessment by an independent third party. A cloud provider's certificate can serve as a reference for obtaining your own certification.
diffEn: SOC 2 is a report in which an auditor evaluates the design and operating effectiveness of controls. ISMS differs in that it certifies the management mechanism against the standard.
aiEn: Because certification is obtained for each scope of target services, check whether the generative AI service you use is within the scope. Your own certification is needed separately.

defEn: A set of controls for cyber defence developed by the non-profit organisation CIS (Center for Internet Security) by consensus. They are mapped to standards such as NIST CSF and the ISO 27000 series.
howEn: Controls are numbered and are referred to by section numbers such as “3.11”. The Microsoft cloud security benchmark maps its own controls to the numbers of CIS Controls v8.1 (example: encryption at rest is 3.11).
diffEn: CIS Benchmarks are configuration standards for individual products (Level 1 and 2), and each recommendation refers to the CIS Controls. The CSF is a framework of outcomes, and CIS Controls is on the side of concrete controls.
aiEn: Microsoft's AI security controls (use of approved models AI-1, AI red teaming AI-7, and so on) are also mapped to the numbers of CIS Controls v8.1.

fullEn: System and Organization Controls 2 (internal control report for service organisations)
defEn: A report in which a third party evaluates the controls of a service organisation against the criteria of security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy, based on the framework of the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA).
howEn: The auditor evaluates the description of the system and the controls. Type I covers the design of controls at a specific point in time, and Type II covers the design and operating effectiveness over a period of time. The gap from the end of the reporting period to the user's period end is covered by management's bridge letter.
diffEn: Whereas ISMS certification is certification of the management mechanism, SOC 2 is a report for users to evaluate the risk of an outsourced provider. Responses to exceptions are also included in the report.
aiEn: When procuring an AI service, check whether the service is within the scope of the report, the period covered, the exceptions, and the controls that the user side should implement (User Entity Responsibilities).

fullEn: Information system Security Management and Assessment Program (security assessment scheme for government information systems)
defEn: A scheme that assesses and registers in advance cloud services that satisfy the security requirements demanded by the government, aiming to secure the security level in government cloud procurement and to enable smooth adoption. Registered services are published in the ISMAP Cloud Service List.
howEn: The provider builds controls according to the ISMAP Management Criteria (incorporating the JIS Q 27000 series, the Government Unified Standards and NIST SP800-53), and undergoes an external audit by a registered audit organisation and an examination by the operations support organisation (IPA). Whether to register is decided by the steering committee, and the process is repeated every year.
diffEn: ISMAP-LIU is a framework for SaaS used for low-risk operations and information. Whereas ISMS certification and SOC 2 reports are private-sector third-party evaluations, ISMAP is a list registration scheme for government procurement.
aiEn: Government agencies and the like, as a rule, procure from the ISMAP Cloud Service List. When proposing a cloud-based generative AI service for the public sector, whether it is registered is a point to check.

fullEn: METI Cybersecurity Management Guidelines Ver 3.0 (Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and IPA)
defEn: Guidelines by the Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry and IPA, aimed at executives, that compile the 3 principles executives should recognise and the 10 important items they should instruct the responsible officer (CISO, etc.) to address. Ver 3.0 was published on 24 March 2023 (Reiwa 5).
howEn: The 3 principles are executive leadership, attention to the whole supply chain, and communication with internal and external parties in both normal times and emergencies. The 10 items give instructions covering policy formulation, management structure, securing resources, risk response, PDCA, emergency response and recovery structure, the supply chain, information sharing and so on.
diffEn: It is not a collection of controls listing individual technical measures (such as CIS Controls) but a document that sets out executives' responsibilities and items to instruct. IPA separately publishes a collection of practices for implementation.
aiEn: The policy, structure and emergency response for risks that come with introducing generative AI can be explained to senior management within the framework of the 10 items and used as material for obtaining approval.

fullEn: Risk Assessment / Risk Treatment (risk evaluation and response)
defEn: The process of estimating the magnitude of risk from the threats, vulnerabilities and impacts for the information assets to be protected, and judging by comparison with risk criteria whether it is acceptable, together with the choice among avoidance, reduction, transfer and acceptance according to the result.
howEn: The approaches are baseline, which uses existing standards; informal, which relies on experience; detailed risk analysis, which looks at asset value, threats and vulnerabilities for each asset; and combinations of these. Detailed analysis proceeds in the order of identifying assets, calculating risk values and deciding on measures. Exceptions such as acceptance require the approval of management.
diffEn: A vulnerability assessment is a means of finding technical flaws, whereas risk assessment is the process of combining those results with the importance of assets and with threats to decide the priority of responses.
aiEn: For generative AI, identify the sensitivity of input data and the scope of integration destinations as information assets. The Financial Services Agency's guidelines also call for risk assessment when providing new products and services.

fullEn: Information Security Policy (basic policy, countermeasure standards and implementation procedures)
defEn: A system of regulations documenting an organisation's policy and how it protects itself, in whose formulation senior management is involved. It is organised through the relationship among the basic policy, the countermeasure standards (standards to be observed) and the implementation procedures (concrete procedures for individual operations and systems).
howEn: Based on the basic policy, countermeasure standards are defined in light of the results of risk assessment, and implementation procedures for carrying them out in individual operations and systems are prepared. The responsible person decides after deliberation by a committee, and the policy is reviewed in response to changes in the environment. The Financial Services Agency's guidelines call for regulations to be reviewed at least once a year.
diffEn: Whereas the government's Unified Standards are common compliance requirements for agencies and the like to observe, countermeasure standards are documents that define concrete measures to suit the characteristics of the organisation itself. Different measures are acceptable if they are of an equivalent or higher level.
aiEn: Rules for using generative AI (available tools, information that may be entered, approval procedures) can be kept consistent by adding to the existing countermeasure standards and implementation procedures rather than creating a separate new document.

nameEn: Third-party risk management (outsourced providers and the supply chain)
fullEn: Third-Party Risk Management / Cyber Supply Chain Risk Management (C-SCRM)
defEn: An effort to manage, consistently from selection through to contract termination, cybersecurity risks originating from third parties and the supply chain, such as outsourced providers, cloud providers and the suppliers of products and services.
howEn: Third parties are managed in a register (services provided, level of access to systems, type and location of data handled), and risk is assessed according to importance. Due diligence is performed before the transaction, the contract states the demarcation of responsibility, audit rights, subcontracting, incident reporting and data handling, and monitoring is continuous.
diffEn: Whereas the shared responsibility model shows how responsibility is divided between the cloud provider and the customer, third-party risk management refers to the whole management mechanism from selecting business partners through contracts and monitoring to termination.
aiEn: In procuring AI models and SaaS as well, the arrangements for the location, storage and disposal of data, the subcontracting procedures, and checking third-party assurance reports (SOC 2, etc.) can be made evaluation items.

nameEn: Security control measures under the Act on the Protection of Personal Information
fullEn: Security control measures based on the Act on the Protection of Personal Information (Personal Information Protection Commission guidelines)
defEn: The necessary and appropriate measures that a personal information handling business operator takes to prevent leakage and the like of personal data. The content is decided according to the magnitude of the infringement of the rights and interests of the individual, the scale and nature of the business, the handling situation and so on.
howEn: The attachment to the guidelines sets out formulation of a basic policy, establishment of rules for handling, 4 types of measures (organisational, human, physical and technical), and understanding of the external environment. The example methods do not all have to be adopted. Supervision of outsourced providers through selection, contracts and understanding of how they handle data is also required.
diffEn: Whereas ISMS is voluntary certification for business operators, these are measures that the law requires of business operators that handle personal data. Reporting to the Commission when a leakage or the like occurs is also stipulated.
aiEn: When having an external AI service handle personal data, supervision of the outsourced provider and, when it is handled in a foreign country, understanding the external environment (checking that country's system) become issues.

nameEn: Cybersecurity guidelines for the financial sector
fullEn: Guidelines for Cybersecurity in the Financial Sector (Financial Services Agency, 4 October 2024; Reiwa 6)
defEn: A document in which the Financial Services Agency sets out supervisory points of focus on the cybersecurity management systems of financial institutions and the like. It is organised in the order of governance, identification, protection, detection, response and recovery, and third-party risk management, and became applicable on 4 October 2024 (Reiwa 6).
howEn: Each item is divided into “basic items for action”, covering fundamentals such as cyber hygiene, and advanced “items for which action is desirable”, which large institutions and the like should refer to. In neither case is a uniform response expected; the premise is a risk-based approach in which the organisation identifies and assesses its own risks and takes commensurate measures.
diffEn: Whereas the METI Cybersecurity Management Guidelines present 3 principles and 10 items for executives, these target financial institutions and the like and make concrete the points of focus that the Financial Services Agency uses in inspections and monitoring.
aiEn: Even outside financial institutions, it can serve as a reference example for conducting risk assessments once a year, for assessing new products and services, and for gauging the level of third-party management.

fullEn: Security and Privacy Controls for Information Systems and Organizations (NIST SP 800-53 Rev.5)
defEn: A catalogue of security and privacy controls for information systems and organisations, published by the US NIST. With Rev.5, the security and privacy controls became a single integrated catalogue.
howEn: Rev.5 changed the description of controls to an outcome basis that does not depend on the entity that satisfies them (system or organisation), and separated the control selection process from the main body. A control family for supply chain risk management (SCRM) was newly established, and that perspective was also built into the catalogue as a whole.
diffEn: Whereas the NIST CSF presents a framework for an organisation's cyber risk management, SP 800-53 is a catalogue containing the individual controls.
aiEn: When the explanations of US government-related customers or of cloud and AI vendors are expressed in terms of these control names, it can be used to map them to your own controls. The fact that SCRM now stands on its own is a useful reference for procurement management.

fullEn: Cloud security controls (27017), protection of PII in the cloud (27018), privacy information management (27701)
defEn: A group of standards that, on the foundation of ISO/IEC 27001 and 27002, add guidance on cloud-specific controls (27017), PII protection in public clouds (27018) and a privacy information management system (27701).
howEn: 27017 adds cloud-specific guidance to the 37 controls of 27002, and adds controls such as division of responsibilities, return and deletion of assets at contract termination, and separation of customer environments. 27018 is for cloud providers that are PII processors. 27701 is an extension of 27001 and cannot obtain certification on its own.
diffEn: Whereas ISMS (27001) covers an organisation's information security as a whole, these are extensions specialised in the cloud and the handling of personal information. Certification to 27701 cannot be regarded as proof of GDPR compliance.
aiEn: In selecting AI and SaaS providers, it is material for checking whether certification exists and the scope of the services covered. Certification does not guarantee that your own usage configuration complies, and your own assessment is needed separately.
